ARI 201LEC - Arabic Second Year-First Semester

Expands on language skills mastered in ARI 101/ ARI 111 and ARI 102 /ARI 112. Reviewsboth basic and complex grammatical and pronunciation patterns, and provides intensive vocabulary expansion through a variety of readings, as well as conversation and writing practice.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Pre-Requisite: ARI 102 / ARI 112 or equivalent.
title: ARI 201LEC - Arabic Second Year-First Semester

html:
PSY 401LEC - Personality Disorders

This course will explore theory, classification, assessment, and treatment of personality pathology, which is an important and impactful form of psychopathology.  These topics will be covered from the perspective of the patient, the practicing clinician, as well as the research scientist.  Theories of etiology, classification, and treatment of these disorders will be focused on those having a strong evidence base.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Psychology majors only, 45 credits completerd and completion of at least one 300-level PSY course.
title: PSY 401LEC - Personality Disorders

html:
AMS 265LEC - Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Social Justice in the United States

This course will use various disciplinary perspectives to examine the nature and meaning of race and Indigeneity in American society. These disciplinary lenses include history, sociology, indigeneity studies, gender and sexuality studies, literary criticism, and film studies. We seek to understand that race as it is presented to us is of recent origin, and that it emerges from strains of thought from Europe and North America over the course of roughly three centuries. We focus on race as a social and cultural category and the ways it shapes contemporary American life.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: AMS 265LEC - Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Social Justice in the United States

html:
IDS 362SEM - Indigenous Data Sovereignty

Grounded in long-standing Indigenous struggles against historical and ongoing colonization and building upon our Indigenous rights to data stewardship under international law (circa 2007’s UNDRIP), Indigenous Data Sovereignty (IDSov) emerged in the 2010s as a framework that ensures Indigenous access and control over data about our peoples, territories, lifeways, and resources. After a primer on Indigeneity and the problems of colonial racialization and Indigenous elimination in Indigenous statistics, this course dives into a survey of the burgeoning landscape of IDSov initiatives emerging across the Anglophone settler-colonial states (Aotearoa New Zealand, Australia, Canada, and the United States), with a particular emphasis on the political economy of IDSov in Indigenous nonprofits in the continental US.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: IDS 362SEM - Indigenous Data Sovereignty

html:
ITA 225LEC - Italy and Italian Cinema: Global Contexts, Past and Present

This course is an introduction to the exceptionality of Italian cinema. Students will become familiar with the poetics and histories of Italian cinema while developing perspectives on Italian history from the twentieth century to the present. In the first part of the semester students will watch several films and learn to identify key features of Italian cinema, while also exploring twentieth-century Italian history. In the second part of the semester students will discuss and compare these films with contemporary Italian ones that overtly assume motifs, themes and styles of previous Italian “classical” films, considering how these newer films relaunch the force of the previous poetics in and for our contemporary globalized time. Across the course, students will be exposed to a panoramic presentation of Italian cinema, illuminating both its specificity and its impact at a global scale. Focal topics will include work, inequality and economic “miracles,” climate change and ecology, question of genre, feminism and the gendered gazes, and immigration and migration. Taught in English, the course will fulfill the Global and Thematic Pathways/UB Curriculum.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: ITA 225LEC - Italy and Italian Cinema: Global Contexts, Past and Present

html:
COM 416LEC - Computer-Mediated Communication

The proliferation of technology raises interesting questions regarding the impact these communication channels have on individuals and their relationships. This course examines the foundational theories and methodologies used to investigate human interaction via communication technology, also known as computer-mediated communication (CMC). After taking this course, you will be familiar with these technologies’ theoretical and methodological evolution and how they impact individuals on an intrapersonal, interpersonal, and global scale.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: COM 416LEC - Computer-Mediated Communication

html:
PSY 400LEC - Prosocial Motivation

From caring for young to (mostly) obeying laws, people routinely place the good of others or society ahead of their immediate gratification. What motivates these behaviors is the focus of this course. We will read and critically discuss recent and classic research addressing these motivations and the diverse contexts in which they play out. Course work will include lectures, small group discussions, and the development of student research proposals.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
PSY 101 , PSY 331
title: PSY 400LEC - Prosocial Motivation

html:
TH 327LEC - Seriously Funny: Comedy In Text And Performance

This course surveys the evolution of comedy in performance over the last 100 years. Students will explore the mechanics of constructing comedy through text and performance in styles such as Vaudeville, Variety/Sketch Comedy, Situation Comedy, Stand-Up, 20th Century Farce, Improv, Post-Seinfeld Irony, and Front-Facing Camera/Social Media Comedy. Modern forms will be compared to texts from historical genres such as Old and New Comedy, Comedy of Humours, Comedy of Manners, Commedia and Humanism, Satire, and Victorian Farce. Theories of play as an essential aspect of the human experience will be considered, as well as the influence of class systems, politics and technology on the evolution of comedy.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: TH 327LEC - Seriously Funny: Comedy In Text And Performance

html:
PSC 203LEC - AI and Democracy

The rise of language learning models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) has drastically changed several facets of society. Government is no exception to this, as these new technologies have already begun to work their way into governmental institutions around the world. This brings us to the questions of this course - how does and how will AI impact democracy as a system of government? Does AI make states more democratic, or does it push them towards authoritarianism?

Students can expect to learn about different types of AIs, different types of democratic systems and institutions, and then apply that knowledge to various policy areas. We will examine how AI modifies the calculations for war, what human rights for AIs would look like, and how democracies can wield AIs in both positive and negative fashions. By the end of the semester, students should walk away from this class with an understanding of the importance of AI on democratic systems.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: PSC 203LEC - AI and Democracy

html:
ASL 499TUT - American Sign Language Independent Study

This course provides an opportunity for students to explore and engage with a topic of their choice in the American Sign Language (ASL) field of study, which is not covered in regular course offerings. The course also allows students to design a new course that is not currently offered in the ASL program and complete it over one semester. Lastly, independent studies are not intended to replace required ASL courses, although exceptions may be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Credits: 1-6

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring, Summer

Requisites:
ASL 111  and ASL 112
title: ASL 499TUT - American Sign Language Independent Study

html:
RLL 323SEM - Gender and Pre-Modern Medicine

This class focuses on how issues of gender and sexuality have been addressed by pre-modern medicine on a global scale. It addresses medical notions of gendered bodies and their changes throughout history, taking into consideration a variety of cultural traditions. It also explores the presence of women in the medical arts, in their different roles of patients, objects of investigation on the part of male doctors, caretakers, and unrecognized practitioners of medicine until their final recognition as legitimate interlocutors for male scientists. This course is the same as GGS 323  and repeat rules may apply. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)
title: RLL 323SEM - Gender and Pre-Modern Medicine

html:
GGS 392SEM - Italian Food: Culture, Health, Sustainability, Marketing

This course explores the tradition of Italian food examining its profound interconnection with Italian culture. It pays attention to the regional varieties of Italian food, to the Italian-American culinary tradition, and to how food has shaped Italian society. Italian food is analyzed within the broader tradition of the Mediterranean diet, with a reflection on its benefits, and healthy nutrition. The course introduces students to the “Slow Food” movement and to its investigation of questions of sustainability and respect for the environment. Finally, it devotes attention to the dynamics, and the marketing and business strategies of Italian food abroad (with specific attention to local imports in Western NY). This is the same course as ITA 392   and repeat rules may apply. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: GGS 392SEM - Italian Food: Culture, Health, Sustainability, Marketing

html:
GGS 206SEM - Indigenous Women: History and Theory

Critically examines the histories, contributions, and challenges of North American Indigenous women. Takes an intersectional approach that attends to gender, indigeneity, and settler colonialism in understanding Indigenous women’s realities and concerns. Exposure to new methodologies that center Indigenous women’s experience in historical analysis and cultural critiques. This course is the same as IDS 206   and repeat rules may apply. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)
title: GGS 206SEM - Indigenous Women: History and Theory

html:
COM 245LEC - Communication and Sports

This course provides students with an overview of various aspects of the relationship between communication (especially, media) and sports. Topics covered may include the history of mediated sports; how various communication industries program, report, and promote sports and athletes; the audiences who consume mediated sports; and various social issues (e.g., sexual identity, race/ethnicity, politics, criminality) raised, perpetuated, or critiqued by sports coverage.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: COM 245LEC - Communication and Sports

html:
AI 101LEC - AI & Society

This course is an introduction to the study of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Society. Through the examination of case studies covering all sectors of society, it provides a balanced consideration of the advantages and disadvantages of using AI to advance the public good.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: AI 101LEC - AI & Society

html:
ART 214STU - Digital Photography for Non-Majors

This introductory course for non-art majors covers the fundamentals of digital photography. Students will learn to capture, edit, organize, and share images while exploring the cultural significance and history of photography. Class time combines hands-on practice with group discussions, encouraging students to rethink their approach to photography as an intentional, thoughtful process. The course also teaches practical skills using digital cameras, scanners, and editing tools like Adobe Camera Raw, Bridge, and Photoshop, with a focus on experimentation.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: ART 214STU - Digital Photography for Non-Majors

html:
BCH 420LEC - Genetics of Metabolic Disorder

This course offers an advance, in-depth look at how and why symptoms of metabolic disorders manifest due to genetic variations in genes expressed within cells or tissues. Overarching goals of this course are to help students understand why genetic variants do not affect all cell types equally despite pathways being common to most cells, and how a mutation that affects one tissue can result in major issues for other tissues.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: BCH 403  and BCH 410
title: BCH 420LEC - Genetics of Metabolic Disorder

html:
BIO 131LAB - Myths and Monsters Lab

Myths and monsters are fun to talk about, but how do you separate fact from fiction? In this laboratory we will evaluate a wide variety of evidence to determine if zombies are alive, whether monsters like Godzilla, Mothra, and King Kong are possible, and the ecological reasons why ‘cryptic species’ like bigfoot and the Loch Ness monster are unlikely to exist. We will examine the reality of genetic mutations, genetic engineering, and evolution to better understand which depictions of these biological processes in movies are and are not grounded in science. Topics will be explored through labs, which will require students to evaluate evidence with the goal of building scientific literacy to help separate science fact from science fiction

Credits: 1

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Corequisite: BIO 131
title: BIO 131LAB - Myths and Monsters Lab

html:
COL 115LEC - Genocide, Testimony, Truth

The term “genocide” emerged in the aftermath of World War II to designate criminal acts carried out with the intent to destroy national, ethnic, racial or religious groups. In this context, genocide has often been considered the paradigmatic “crime against humanity” and the “crime of crimes.” The term continues to be relevant for international law today. Focusing on the legacy of the concept, the course addresses the historical parameters of genocide by examining the Nazi genocide of the European Jewish population and the Rwandan genocide of 1994. At the heart of the course, however, is the tension between historical truth and testimony, on the one hand, that the relation of both to fictional accounts. Fulfills SUNY GE in Humanities and World History and Global Awareness. This course is the same as JDS 115 and course repeat rules will apply. Students should consult with their major department regarding any restrictions on their degree requirements. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: COL 115LEC - Genocide, Testimony, Truth

html:
COM 458SEM - AI as Medium & Communicator

How is AI shaking up our society, for better or worse? What differentiates AI tools from social companions? With all its potential, do you want to be a passive or a proactive user of AI? This course will cover different roles, unique capabilities, and important implications of AI through lectures, activities, skill labs, and a capstone project. Students will (1) gain key knowledge about the evolution and applications of AI; (2) critically assess the benefits and harms of AI in ongoing ethical debates; (3) learn communication theories and media effects research to understand human-AI interactions; and (4) master hands-on skills to enhance their academic and professional growth.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: COM 458SEM - AI as Medium & Communicator

html:
CSE 465LEC - Computer Security

This course introduces students to fundamentals of computer and information security, with the goals of developing a solid understanding of the principles of the security field and building knowledge of tools and mechanisms to safeguard a wide range of software and computing systems. Topics covered in the course include cryptographic background and tools, access control, authentication, software security, malware, Internet security protocols and standards (TLS, IPsec, etc.), intrusion detection and intrusion prevention systems (firewalls), database security, privacy, security management and risk assessment, and legal and ethical aspects (cybercrime, intellectual property). The course generally covers similar topics to those covered in CSE 365, but doesn’t spend as much time on the background and goes into more depth. The expected background is algorithms’ complexity, systems, and networking basics.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
 CSE 220 ,  CSE 250 , and  CSE 365  OR CSE 312  OR CSE 489 . School of Engineering and Applied Sciences majors only.
title: CSE 465LEC - Computer Security

html:
DMS 300LEC - 16mm Film Production

This course introduces students to the creative use of analog 16mm film in conventional and unconventional ways. With the advent of digital video, many were eulogizing the death of film. However, over thirty years later, it thrives. With advocacy from big-name directors like Christopher Nolan and Quentin Tarantino, film remains a coveted medium in studio productions. At the same time, independent and experimental filmmakers continue to explore and broaden film’s possibilities. The bright pixels of digital video make for captivating imagery, but there’s a unique beauty to the swirl of grain on celluloid. In addition to the aesthetic appeal of physical, mechanical, and chemical reproduction, students gain a deeper understanding of the origins and operation of any camera and how an actual frame, shutter, and aperture function. Shooting on film requires a more thoughtful, structured approach that positively informs any kind of media making one does whether analog or digital. 

This class covers the basics of shooting and hand-processing 16mm film with an introduction to other alternative techniques. In-class workshops, take-home assignments, and a final project are supplemented by screenings and readings. Students will receive some supplies but may need to spend additionally on stock and processing. Lab fee.

Credits: 4

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Prerequisite: DMS 103
title: DMS 300LEC - 16mm Film Production

html:
EE 451LEC - Intro to 2D Electronics

This course is designed to introduce emerging 2D materials (e.g., graphene, MoS2, h-BN etc.) and their electronic properties to advanced undergraduate students. The course will cover both fundamental knowledge and cutting-edge technology of 2D materials, and will give a comparative study with traditional 3D semiconductor physics. The main course includes electronic structures and properties, synthesis and characterization, engineering and application of 2D materials and their heterostructures. The course also includes several lab sessions so the students can participate in hands-on experiments under supervision.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Every Other Fall

Requisites:
It is recommended to have taken EE 421  and EE 430  before enrolling in EE 451. Engineering Majors or Electrical Engineering Minors Only.
title: EE 451LEC - Intro to 2D Electronics

html:
ITE 496TUT - Global Experience Internship

The Global Experience Internship program provides undergraduate students with immersive, hands-on experience in professional work environments, including opportunities in Singapore and beyond. Through structured workplace experiences that complement their academic studies, students apply classroom knowledge to real-world challenges while developing essential cross-cultural competencies. The program welcomes students from diverse academic disciplines and encourages exploration of both major-related and interdisciplinary opportunities. Working collaboratively with faculty advisors and workplace supervisors, students engage in guided reflection activities to deepen their professional capabilities, enhance their global perspective, and build valuable networks that strengthen their career prospects in an increasingly interconnected world.

Credits: 1-3

Grading
Pass/Not Pass

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring, Summer

Requisites:
Junior or senior class standing required, with good academic standing.
title: ITE 496TUT - Global Experience Internship

html:
COM 474SEM - Intercultural Communication & Cross-Cultural Adaptation

In this course students learn intercultural communication principles, theories, and research methodologies while interacting and building relationships with individuals from other countries. Throughout the course students have the opportunity to reflect on their own culture and experiences and better understand the roots of cultural similarities and differences. In addition, students develop an awareness of how cultural identity influences the communication process and prepare to become more effective communicators both in their home country and abroad.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: COM 474SEM - Intercultural Communication & Cross-Cultural Adaptation

JDS 115LEC - Genocide, Testimony, Truth

The term “genocide” emerged in the aftermath of World War II to designate criminal acts carried out with the intent to destroy national, ethnic, racial or religious groups. In this context, genocide has often been considered the paradigmatic “crime against humanity” and the “crime of crimes.” The term continues to be relevant for international law today. Focusing on the legacy of the concept, the course addresses the historical parameters of genocide by examining the Nazi genocide of the European Jewish population and the Rwandan genocide of 1994. At the heart of the course, however, is the tension between historical truth and testimony, on the one hand, that the relation of both to fictional accounts. Fulfills SUNY GE in Humanities and World History and Global Awareness.This course is the same as COL 115  and course repeat rules will apply. students should consult with their major department regarding any restrictions on their degree requirement.

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: JDS 115LEC - Genocide, Testimony, Truth

html:
AI 102LLR - Introduction to Computational Fundamentals: Programming, Machines, and Constructing Knowledge

This course introduces students to a breadth of topics that underpin how computing devices function in our modern world. Students will also learn how computing systems are connected and work together to form the digital infrastructure we use in our daily lives, explore their potential impacts, and contribute to a computing culture that is collaborative and ethical. Students will learn to design and evaluate solutions and to apply computational principles to solve problems through the development of algorithms and programs. Students will learn about how data encode information and how to process that information to inform computing processes.

Credits: 4

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: AI 102LLR - Introduction to Computational Fundamentals: Programming, Machines, and Constructing Knowledge

html:
AI 104LR - Introduction to Computational Expression

This course is designed to introduce freshman and sophomore undergraduate students to the technical and societal workings of programming languages in artificial intelligence (AI). Programming languages are expressions of the mathematics developers need to create, train, and deploy AI systems of all kinds. Students in this course will not be learning a variety of programming languages, though a few will be explored lightly.  This course explores the why of programming: the logic that makes it necessary (so far). The course introduces students to mathematical concepts integral to AI, such as probability, statistics, and gradient descent and invites them to think about why programming languages are needed for the development of AI.  At the end of the course, students will have a basic understanding of why programming works, will have independently used the programming software jupyter notebooks, and will be able to identify basic python libraries for training a handful of AI models on their own machine.

APY 413SEM - Men and Masculinities

This course asks what it means to be a man and/or masculine in the particular context of Euro-American societies. Moving away from the notion of sex and/or gender as reducible to, or primarily determined through biology, we will critically evaluate and analyze how men and masculinities are socially and historically contingent, relationally constructed, diverse, and changing over time periods and in changing contexts. We will focus on how notions and ideas, norms and practices related to what it means to be a man emerge at the intersections of various and dynamic positionalities that individuals may occupy such as age, race, sexuality, health status, and life course, and how these in turn represent men and masculinities in ways that affect individual and group experiences. Thus, men are as much gendered beings as are women. The overall aims of this course are to a. engage with material that directs our attention to the precarity of masculinity i.e., how masculinity is not fixed in its definitions or practices; b. highlight how masculinities derive meaning in relation to (other masculinities/women); and c. how structures (policies, law, representations in scientific literature, medicine and technology) play a key role in reproducing as well as shifting dominant notions of masculinities.

COM 123LR - Numerical Reasoning for Everyday Communication

COM 123 is designed for students at the University who are either uncomfortable with numbers/mathematics or simply dislike having to sort out numbers and compute answers to questions involving numbers. The inability to deal comfortably with numbers, probability, and statistics is often called innumeracy and was popularized by a book by Paulos (1988). Also, called quantitative literacy, the ability to understand the basic principles of numbers is vital to everyday communication and is relevant to our personal and professional lives. This course endeavors to convince students of the importance of numeracy and to teach students the basic aspects of quantitative reasoning. Just as important as numeracy is reasoning that often accompanies the principles of quantitative literacy. That is, one must be able to use and understand the principles in reasoning and decision-making. It is understood that the real world often has less than perfect data, ambiguities (some strategic) and multiple possible solutions that are quantitative in nature. As stipulated on the course schedule and in course outcomes, students will learn an array of quantitative/mathematical methods to reinforce methods they may have already learned and/or to introduce them to methods, models, and data analytical techniques new to them and shown in real-life applications. These include but are not limited to: (1) linear algebra, (2) introductory calculus methods, (3) advanced statistics (e.g., multiple regression, analysis of covariance), (4) graph theory (e.g., through social network analysis), (5) discrete math concepts/set theory, and (6) probability (e.g., conjunction vs. disjunction). It is the expectation of this course that students will be able to, at a minimum, be able to understand and compute basic descriptive statistics, probabilities, compound interest, correlation coefficients, chi-square analysis, and some basic social network math related to relative network position in a closed network. 

Credits: 4

Building on the foundations of COM 225 (Interpersonal Communication), in this course you will learn about the scientific studies of relationships. Sometimes, empirical research can validate what we know. Other times, it can lead to surprising and counterintuitive discovery. You will also learn why we need to study relationships empirically, and how researchers study them. Further, we will discuss how we can implement what we learn in class to promote healthier relationships in our lives. We will deepen our understanding by delving into personal experiences and theoretical perspectives.

AI 325LEC - AI & The Information Environment

Today, more than ever before, we live in an all-around, 24/7, media-saturated world, and recent innovations in AI will potentially change our interaction with information in fundamental ways. In this course, we will consider AI as medium used for communication. To do so, we will situate AI in within the broader narrative or mass communication, and as a continuation of prior innovations, including writing, printing, radio, TV, websites, mobile phones, and video games. We will learn about (1) the history, (2) audience, (3) production, and (4) effects of mass communication in general, and AI in particular. Afterward, distributed machine learning techniques, such as federated learning, will be covered. In the latter topic, the course will focus on the applications of machine learning methods (mostly reinforcement learning) to improve the efficiency of emerging wireless networks. Students will write one midterm and one final paper to be presented in support of audio projects. Participants will develop field recording strategies and audio editing technique, to construct projects as a basis for finding and articulating the “voice” of a site, orienting our critical inquiry and active investigation to engage uses of sound as an artistic medium in the form of ecological research. CSE 406LEC - Blockchain, Cryptocurrency and Decentralized Finance Systems

This course is intended for students interested in learning about blockchain, cryptocurrency, and decentralized finance systems. The course will cover the essentials of blockchain and cryptocurrency and explore the area of Decentralized Finance (DeFi) systems in detail. The course content is divided into three parts: (i) blockchain essentials, (ii) digital assets, and (iii) DEX protocols and platforms, including applications of web3 and DeFi to modernize business systems. The topics covered in the first part of the course include decentralized identity, wallet technology, peer-to-peer transactions, blocks, chain of blocks, smart contracts, web3, and decentralized applications (DApp). These concepts will be illustrated using the Ethereum blockchain. The second part of the course covers digital assets and includes a discussion of cryptocurrencies, tokens, tokenization, fungible, non-fungible, and multi-token, as well as their applications. The concepts will be reinforced using Ethereum’s ERC tokens and real-world assets (RWA) tokens. The course’s third part deals with decentralized exchange (DEX) protocols and platforms, newer models for liquidity, market and market making, and perpetual derivatives. The course will also discuss approaches for introducing web3 and DeFi concepts into existing businesses and systems. Students will work on hands-on projects on Ethereum testnets and simulated environments to reinforce the concepts discussed. On completion of the course, a student will be able to analyze a problem and develop and implement an end-to-end DeFi system to solve a real-world problem.

IDS 354SEM - Indigenous & Black Carcerality and Abolition

Since its inception, the United States has been concerned with projects of dispossession and containment. Modern policing and its consequent mass incarceration exist as examples of such projects. For Indigenous and Black peoples this has been especially apparent and has had an outsize impact on these communities. This course examines the US as a carceral state and necropolitical apparatus marking particular bodies for death and dismemberment (of bodies, of families, of communities). Through the lens of contemporary and historical accounts of policing, it will trace histories of enslavement and land dispossession across time and space to explore mass incarceration, policing, and other forms of state violence. It will also make the important turn of concentrating on contemporary abolition movements aimed to account for these historical circumstances. In so doing, it will also explore connections between Blackness and Indigeneity, Black and Indigenous peoples, and Black liberation and Indigenous sovereignty movements as a means to imagine how abolition can lead us to futures constructed on alternative structures of justice.

MGM 421LEC - Current Issues in Retailing & Omnichannel Commerce Marketing

Retailing is the set of business activities that adds value to products and services sold to consumers. These retailing activities can take place in a variety of areas including in stores, online, social networks, mobile apps, via a salesperson, catalogs or kiosks. Retailers link manufacturers to consumers. Retailers add value by providing an assortment of products and services, offering products in smaller quantities tailored to individuals, holding inventory so the product is available when the customer wants it, and providing services to make it easier for customers to buy and use products.

The objective of this course is to familiarize students with current issues in retailing and omnichannel commerce marketing which involves identifying the target market, the nature of merchandise or services that will be offered to meet the needs of the target market, and how to develop unique assets to achieve long-term advantage over competitors. To understand this, the course focuses on current retail trends, understanding consumers and financial objectives, and examining assets and decisions that allow the retailer to build strategic advantage including location, merchandising, pricing, promotions, omnichannel, retail productivity, commerce marketing, private labels, and loyalty programs.

LAW 415LEC - Legal Procedure for NYS Civil, NYS Criminal and Federal Practice

This course provides an overview of the procedural aspects of civil and criminal actions and proceedings in New York State and Federal Courts. The New York Civil component will address the jurisdiction and function of the State’s various courts (Town, Village, County, Supreme, Family, Surrogate and Appellate levels) and legal concepts such as statute of limitations, service of process, pleadings, discovery, motions and filing of papers (including the NYS Electronic Filing System). The focus will be on New York Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) and Uniform Trial Court Rules. Substantive law will be used to expand the students’ knowledge and provide context. The New York Criminal component will discuss criminal law including frequently seen criminal offenses, common search and seizure issues. Reading noteworthy court decisions, students will learn how a criminal case moves through the court system.  The Federal section will focus on the structure of the federal courts through review of case law and lectures. Topics covered include: the differences between a District Judge and a Magistrate Judge; the stages of a federal criminal prosecution; the role of the U.S. Attorney’s Office and the Federal Public Defender’s Office; and the scope of federal court jurisdiction over civil matters.

ITA 223LEC - Goal! Soccer in Italian and Global Culture and Society

Soccer, the most popular sport in Italy and one of the most popular in the world, is more than just a game. Deeply intertwined with Italy’s political, social, and cultural evolution, soccer provides a lens through which we can reflect on a range of issues that are both local and global. Starting with the origins of Italian soccer in the late 1800s, this course traces the evolution of the game into the 21st century. It explores the rise of the “Italian school,” its decline in a globalized world, and its rejuvenation with the emergence of women’s soccer. This course examines the uniqueness of the Italian approach to the game, marked by a balance between creativity and defense. It charts how politics has appropriated soccer, from Mussolini to Berlusconi, and delves into the violent world of soccer fandom, the ultras, and their relationship with organized crime. Along with this, it traces the romantic stories of the forgotten Hungarian masters of the inter-war period, the 1980s fairytale of Verona F.C., and the cult of “Saint” Diego Armando Maradona.

In recent decades, increased media attention and the proliferation of anti-trans legislation has led to a more general public awareness of basic concepts, images, and social issues impacting transgender and gender variant people. Alongside these developments, an interdisciplinary field of transgender studies has taken shape since the mid-2000s and has provided a rich existential and theoretical set of resources for addressing the complex gendered, racial, and political stakes of trans and gender variant life and futurity. In dialogue with this field of study, this course addresses topics and themes within the field of transgender studies, including, for example, the functions of the nation-state in the formation, authorization, and negotiation of gender, racial, and other identity categories, and how the surveillance and criminalization of forms of embodiment and desire impact transgender and gender variant people. Lastly, building from the rich and varied forms of cultural expression by trans and gender variant people, the course also examines the experiences and liberatory projects of transgender and gender variant activists and scholars. Built on Black and transnational feminist and queer praxis, disability justice makes intersectional demands for the liberation of bodies rendered abnormal and made sick and disabled in the majority world under heteropatriarchy, colonialism, ethnonationalism, and capitalism. Some key concepts and frameworks include antiblackness and the nonhuman, settler colonial benevolence and rehabilitation, discursive and material disablement, carceral care, and crip of color critique. ENG 439SEM - Rhetorical Theory and Practice

People have been theorizing about, defining, and re-defining rhetoric for more than two thousand years. Rhetoric has been praised as a force for enhancing the commonwealth and criticized as a tool for deceiving the masses. This course conceives of rhetoric as a way for people to achieve important things together if they listen deeply and conscientiously to what each other is saying, but part of your job in this course will be to think through which of the many definitions of (and attitudes toward) rhetoric works best for you. More broadly speaking, rhetoric matters because it is a powerful force for creating change in the world, and it is important both to consider how rhetoric is used to create these changes and how to intervene in these processes. Rhetorical theory and practice are closely intertwined, and in this course we will use theory to improve our rhetorical practice and use practice to better understand rhetorical theory. 
Toward the end of the semester, students will compose a capstone project via which they will circulate what they have learned about rhetoric to audiences beyond the classroom community.

END 314LEC - Immigrants and the City

More people than ever live in a country other than the one they were born in: over 281 million people (about 3.6% of the global population) have left their home country (United Nations, n.d.). Some are forcibly displaced due to conflict, violence, or disasters, while others choose to leave for economic, familial, or educational opportunities. The United States is home to more international migrants than any other nation. About 25% of children under age 18 have a parent who came to the US as an immigrant (Lopez, 2022). International migration is a large driver of urban development, and immigrants have shaped cities since our nations founding. 

This undergraduate course introduces issues arising from the movement of peoples across national boundaries and explores how policy, planning, and the built environment can influence migration and immigrants’ experiences. We start globally, examining push and pull factors that drive migration, along with policy and planning responses to immigrants. In the second half, we focus on immigration in the US. We identify differences and complexities among different immigrant groups and explore responses to immigration. Throughout the course, students will critically examine the possibilities and difficulties of planning for the wellbeing of immigrant populations.

The purpose of this course is to expose students to research being conducted in the Biomedical Sciences. The course will consist of a program of supervised research to be agreed upon by the student and a faculty sponsor with oversight from the program director (Amy Jacobs). 

Credits: 1-6

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring, Summer
title: MIC 498TUT - Undergraduate Research in the Biomedical Sciences

html:
PSY 406LEC - The Social Brain

Why are some animals, including humans, social? Why do we seek out interactions with others and gain comfort from these interactions? Why do we live in groups? This course will examine social behaviors and how they are regulated by the brain. Material is drawn from multiple perspectives, covering concepts from Behavioral Neuroscience, Social Neuroscience, Animal Behavior, Behavioral Ecology, and Evolutionary Biology. We will discuss a diverse set of social behaviors in multiple species - from birds and rodents to humans.

Credits: 3

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Every Other Fall

Requisites:
Psychology majors only.  PSY 351LEC - Biopsychology  and 45 credits completed.
title: PSY 406LEC - The Social Brain

html:
PMY 201LEC - Molecules to Medicines

Molecules to Medicines explores how ideas at the molecular level become real therapies that improve human health. Nearly everyone relies on medications-but how are they discovered, tested, and refined, and why do they work the way they do? In this entry-level course, students are introduced to pharmacology as a discipline that bridges chemistry, biology, medicine, and public health. Through lectures and collaborative and self-directed learning opportunities, students will learn about basic principles that govern drug action, explore current methods and topics in pharmacological research and drug development, and develop teamwork, communication and critical analysis skills essential for entering graduate or health professions programs. The course also highlights the diverse career paths available in pharmacology and related fields, helping students connect course content to future study and employment opportunities

Credits: 2

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: PMY 201LEC - Molecules to Medicines

html:
IE 428LEC - Decision-based System Design

The course is designed for engineering students who are interested in furthering their knowledge in decision making methods during engineering design process. The Decision-Based Design (DBD) approach models design as a decision-making process with the aim of maximizing the performance of a designed artifact. The main question addressed in this course is: ‘what design alternative is the best considering both the performance of the design artifact and the consumer preferences?’ This course emphasizes the role of uncertainty in engineering design and reviews different approaches to decision-based design through discussing the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. Various topics including Robust Design, Suh’s Design Axioms, Multi-Attribute Utility Theory, Discrete Choice Analysis, Simulation-based Approaches, and Analytical Techniques for Modeling Consumer Preferences and Choices will be discussed in this course. Moreover, this course discusses the challenges that decision maker’s irrationalities and cognitive biases can bring into the design process.

Credits: 3

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
School of Engineering and Applied Sciences majors only.
title: IE 428LEC - Decision-based System Design

HON 492SEM - Honors College Think Tank I

This course is a brief introduction to the world of Think Tanks and policy papers. Students will learn about the purpose and structure of policy papers and form working groups on topics of their own choosing, which will continue through the spring semester under the guidance of a faculty advisor. The end product will be a policy paper, presentation poster, and oral presentation of findings. Policy papers will be accessioned to the UB Institutional Repository. 

Credits: 1

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
HON 102 , HON 250 , or HON249
title: HON 492SEM - Honors College Think Tank I

html:
HON 493TUT - Honors College Think Tank II

This course is the second semester of a two-course sequence with HON492 and consists of advanced, faculty-mentored primary research and writing. Working in groups and on topics developed in HON 492  , students will research and write policy papers under the guidance of a faculty advisor. By the end of the semester, students will produce an approximately 10,000-15,000-word long policy paper, and a presentation poster. They will also give an oral presentation of their findings. Policy papers will be accessioned to the UB Institutional Repository.

Credits: 3

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
HON 492SEM - Honors College Think Tank I Credits: 1
title: HON 493TUT - Honors College Think Tank II

SOC 380LEC - Korean Society through K-Movie and K-Drama

This course uses K-movies and K-dramas as a lens to deepen students’ understanding of Korean society. Film and television are powerful tools that reflect and critique social realities, offering insight into both historical and contemporary issues. Through a sociological framework, students will examine Korea’s past and present, as well as the cultural and structural factors that continue to shape Korean society.  Topics include pressing social issues such as class inequality, labor market segmentation, and gender norms, as well as broader historical and cross-national contexts, including the Korean diaspora and the 1997 Asian financial crisis. The course will also explore the global implications of K-movies and K-dramas. By the end of the course, students will gain a sharper understanding of how popular culture illuminates Korea’s social dynamics and resonates beyond national borders.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Occasionally
title: SOC 380LEC - Korean Society through K-Movie and K-Drama

html:
CE 455LEC - Industrial Practices for Chemical Engineers

This course will prepare chemical engineering students for successful careers in industry by providing them with powerful insight into how industry works, the different functions in industry, and what key roles chemical engineers play in them. Examples and case studies from different industries in this highly interactive course will be used. This course will be conducted by people with industrial experience. This will help students with their careers and successful transition to industry. Students will become familiar with their role as a Chemical Engineer by understanding how Product, Process, R&D, External Manufacturing, Technical Support, Quality, Safety and various other functions work in different industries. Additionally, they will learn about how they will use Big Data, Internet of Things (IOT), Generative AI and other new technologies which are rapidly evolving and being adopted in industry, helping to change process control, continuous manufacturing, innovation, and product development.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
CE 212; chemical engineering major or permission of department
title: CE 455LEC - Industrial Practices for Chemical Engineers

html:
MGF 120LEC - Introduction to Financial Markets

This course provides an introductory overview of financial markets and the institutions that shape them. Students will explore how capital moves through the economy, the roles of key market participants, and the broad types of financial instruments and services. The course examines how economic trends, policy decisions, and global events influence markets and introduces core ideas of risk, return, and investment strategy. Students will gain early exposure to industry tools, career pathways, and financial news. Through discussions, case examples, and interactive activities, they will connect foundational concepts to real-world contexts and understand how financial markets support businesses, individuals, and the global economy, preparing them for more advanced study in finance.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: MGF 120LEC - Introduction to Financial Markets

html:
MGF 430LEC - Advanced Financial Planning and Wealth Management

This course is designed for students interested in careers in financial planning, wealth management, portfolio management, banking, and capital markets, as well as those seeking to build lifelong personal finance skills. It focuses on holistic wealth management-managing an individual’s net worth and its risk over a lifetime, incorporating both liquid and illiquid assets, liabilities, and evolving goals. Students will explore how investment decisions adapt to life events, market changes, and personal financial objectives. Emphasis is placed on applying theory to practice through the use of real-world examples, including accounting for taxes, regulations, private investments, mortgages, pensions, and more. Rather than offering prescriptive advice, the students would familiarize themselves with updated market data, dynamic balance sheets, and modeling tools to support disciplined, customized financial decision-making. The course also draws parallels between personal and institutional investment processes, encouraging students to develop critical thinking and practical problem-solving skills in complex financial environments.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisite: MGF 402
title: MGF 430LEC - Advanced Financial Planning and Wealth Management

html:
MGF 432LEC - Fixed Income Securities and Their Markets

This course provides a comprehensive overview of global fixed-income markets and the analytical tools used to evaluate them. Topics include bond pricing and yields, duration and convexity, and the valuation of bonds with embedded options. Students will explore the unique features and risks of a wide range of fixed-income instruments, including government, corporate, asset-backed, and mortgage-backed securities. Additional emphasis is placed on bond price and yield volatility, return decomposition, credit analysis, and yield curve dynamics. While market-focused, the course also aligns with the CFA Level I curriculum on fixed income module, offering valuable preparation for professional certification.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: MGF301 and MGQ301
title: MGF 432LEC - Fixed Income Securities and Their Markets

html:
MGF 434LEC - Valuation and Financial Modeling

This advanced course provides an in-depth exploration of valuation and financial modeling techniques using Microsoft Excel. The course integrates theoretical foundations with practical applications relevant to investment banking, equity research, and corporate finance.  Students will learn to construct fully integrated financial models that connect the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, incorporating both historical and projected data. Core topics include discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation, trading and transaction comparables, and the analysis of key financial ratios. The course also introduces methods for evaluating investment projects. Emphasis is placed on developing proficiency in Excel for financial analysis, forecasting, and presentation. Through applied exercises and real-world case discussions, students will gain the ability to assess corporate performance, test assumptions, and analyze the effects of market events on firm valuation. By the end of the course, students will be able to build comprehensive financial models, interpret valuation outcomes, and apply analytical frameworks to support investment or strategic decisions. Due to the hands-on nature of the course, active participation and consistent attendance are strongly recommended.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: MGF402 or MGF405
title: MGF 434LEC - Valuation and Financial Modeling

html:
MGF 436LEC - Comprehensive Financial Analysis

This course provides an overview of industry practices aligned with the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA®) Candidate Body of Knowledge (CBOK®). It introduces key concepts essential for investment professionals, including ethics and compliance, time value of money, macroeconomics, fixed income and equity valuation, derivatives, capital budgeting, portfolio management, and alternative investments. Emphasis is placed on linking financial theory to real-world practice through discussion of current market trends and events. Students will develop analytical and decision-making skills relevant to careers as securities analysts, portfolio managers, and investment advisors. While the course content supports preparation for the CFA® Level I examination and other professional licensing exams, exam participation is not required. The course provides a foundational understanding of the CFA® framework but does not cover the complete CFA® Level I Candidate Body of Knowledge (CBOK®).

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: MGF402 and MGF405
title: MGF 436LEC - Comprehensive Financial Analysis

html:
MT 433LEC - Forensic Toxicology

This intensive 6-week course provides a comprehensive introduction to forensic toxicology with special emphasis on DUI/DUID investigations and Drug-Facilitated Sexual Assault (DFSA) cases. Students will explore the principles of toxicological analysis in forensic settings, proper sample handling procedures, analytical techniques, data interpretation, and expert testimony. The course covers Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) protocols, the toxicological aspects of impaired driving cases, and the unique challenges presented by DFSA investigations. Through recorded lectures, case studies, and automated assessments, students will develop the fundamental knowledge required for toxicological analysis in forensic and legal contexts.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded

Typically Offered:
Summer

Requisites:
Prerequisites: CHE 203 and CHE 205
title: MT 433LEC - Forensic Toxicology

ES 356LEC - Developing Your Coaching

As a progression of ES256 Principles of Coaching, you will take a deeper dive into sports coaching and enhance your knowledge plus, have the opportunity to practice your coaching skills. The course consists of five modules, each designed to highlight a specific area of sports coaching. Coaches as Culture Keepers, Coaches as Leaders, Coaches as Caregivers, Coaches as Managers, and Coaching Application will enhance your skills and give you the confidence to be a mentor and a leader.

Credits: 3

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
 ES 256
title: ES 356LEC - Developing Your Coaching

UBE 111SEM - Moving Forward

UBE 111 is designed to support students in understanding and navigating the academic, social, financial, and career dimensions of the university experience. This seminar focuses on
reflection, decision-making, self-advocacy, and planning to promote persistence and well-being. 

Credits: 1

Grading
Pass/Not Pass

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: UBE 111SEM - Moving Forward

html:
APY 340LEC - Sports: Culture, Biology, and Heritage

Sports are not just a form of play and entertainment; they are a window into who we are and what we value. In this course we will use an anthropological lens to examine the interactions between culture, biology, and heritage in sports. We will trace the evolution of human biomechanics and the role of cooperation and competition in the past. We will explore sports as a cultural context where we shape perceptions of class, race, sex, gender, and national identity. Sports are also big business, with economic consequences that are felt locally as well as globally. We will examine how sports are highly political, important spaces where policy and social norms are mediated. We will consider sports from across the globe and complement this with a deeper dive into sports and fandom in Buffalo. Whether you are an athlete, a fan, or just curious about the role of sports in our society, this course will encourage you to think critically about how sports impact our lives. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: APY 340LEC - Sports: Culture, Biology, and Heritage

html:
APY 359SEM - Applied Anthropology

This course introduces students to the many ways anthropologists apply their skills beyond the classroom to address real-world issues and improve lives. Through guest speakers, case studies, and reflective exercises, students will explore careers in areas such as public health, UX research, community development, museums, nonprofits, business, and government. Emphasis is placed on identifying the transferable skills gained through anthropology, like cultural analysis, qualitative research, and ethical engagement, and how these skills contribute to social change and innovation. By the end of the seminar, students will be able to articulate potential career paths, connect with practicing anthropologists, and begin developing a personal plan for using anthropology to make a difference in society.

Credits: 1

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: APY 359SEM - Applied Anthropology

BCH 465TUT - Undergraduate Research Proposal

Students will formulate and compose a well-cited research proposal to serve as the foundation for their BCH 498 research. The research mentor will provide students with necessary background papers, assist them in the formulation and discussion of the hypotheses, and provide additional guidance deemed appropriate during the writing process. This course should be completed by the end of their junior year. 

Credits: 1

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Fall, Spring

Co-Requisite: BCH 498  and Permission of Instructor
title: BCH 465TUT - Undergraduate Research Proposal

BMS 301LEC - AI Literacy in the Biomedical Sciences

Literacy in Artificial Intelligence requires the ability to recognize, understand, use and assess computational approaches that collectively comprise artificial intelligence. The goal of this course is to train biomedical scientists to bridge the gap, conceptually, between the biological and computer sciences. In this course we will teach biomedical students to conceptualize problems in healthcare and biomedical research through a computational and data-driven lens. We will teach students the importance of the ethical and informed use of AI and machine learning in biomedical sciences and healthcare through case-based learning. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
BCH 223LEC - Principles of Biomedical Science Credits: 3 , AI 101LEC - AI & Society Credits: 3 , AI 104LR - Introduction to Computational Expression Credits: 4
title: BMS 301LEC - AI Literacy in the Biomedical Sciences

html:
BMS 302LEC - Applications of AI in Biomedical Sciences

Biomedical sciences and healthcare are generating increasingly large datasets. Computational approaches are essential to analyzing these data in a meaningful and timely manner. The goal of this course is to teach students about applications of AI-based approaches in healthcare and biomedical research.  We will provide students with hands-on experience in the application of machine-learning, large language models and agentic approaches to problems including protein structure and drug design, medical imaging, genomics, and healthcare data analytics.   

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Pre-requisites: BMS 301
title: BMS 302LEC - Applications of AI in Biomedical Sciences

html:
BMS 400LEC - Biomedical Image Analysis and AI

This course introduces students to image-based biomedical datasets and the computational tools used to analyze them. Imaging is a fundamental way that humans understand reality, and biomedical imaging relates to nearly every aspect of modern health and research. Students will explore how different imaging modalities (ranging from MRI and CT to microscopy) capture the physical world, and will gain hands-on experience with image processing, feature extraction, annotation, and AI-based analysis. By integrating perspectives from medicine, engineering, and data science, students will learn how biomedical images become data, how AI is transforming this field, and how ethical issues such as patient privacy and annotation bias must be addressed.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Pre-requisites: AI 102 , BMS 301
title: BMS 400LEC - Biomedical Image Analysis and AI

html:
BMS 402LEC - AI Powered Structural Biology and Genomics for Understanding and Treating Cancer

Using cancer as a throughline, this course explores the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across modern biomedicine, from protein structure and its central role in therapeutic development to functional genomics and its importance in understanding cancer predication, development and progression and in developing treatments. Students will learn how AI is revolutionizing our understanding of proteins, gaining hands-on experience with deep learning prediction tools like AlphaFold. The course will explore the underlying biology of cancer development and progression. We will also discuss the methods used to collect different types of data and the complexity and variability of different data sets. The course will then connect these functional molecules to the “blueprints” of life, investigating how AI techniques are applied to foundational genomics research for tasks such as variant calling, gene expression analysis, and disease risk prediction. Finally, students will explore the integration of these structural and genomic insights throughout the modern drug discovery pipeline, from AI-driven target identification and virtual screening to generative models for novel drug design. This course bridges structural biology, genomics, and computational methods, preparing students for careers at the intersection of AI and biomedicine.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Pre-requisites: BCH 403 , BCH 410 , BMS 301 , BMS 302
title: BMS 402LEC - AI Powered Structural Biology and Genomics for Understanding and Treating Cancer

DMS 444SEM - Environmental Media Production

This course is an intensive workshop in environmental media production for graduate students and advanced undergraduates across disciplines. Through readings, screenings, class presentations, and discussions, students will investigate and interrogate an array of approaches to communicating ideas and creating art about the environment and catalyzing social change toward a more sustainable society. We will explore the recent history of creating environmental media in the era of climate chaos, and we will ask what kinds of media we will need in the future to move our societies in the direction of ecological sustainability. Students will develop and create media production projects, related to environmental concerns, in film/time-based media art, podcasting, and visual art, in addition to a final project in the medium of their choice, interpreted broadly, including films, podcasts, photography, visual art, XR, video games, and text. There will be multiple stages of the production projects throughout the semester, and we will workshop each stage in class. This is an advanced production course that requires students to be familiar with the production processes and techniques of a variety of media or be willing to learn them in the course of the class. This course is the same as EVS 444 and course repeat rules will apply. Students should consult with their major department regarding any restrictions on their degree requirements. This course is dual listed with DMS/EVS 544.

Credits: 4

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Prerequisites are any 2 of the following: DMS 302SEM, DMS 341SEM, DMS 342SEM, DMS 343SEM, DMS 401SEM, DMS 402SEM, DMS 404SEM, DMS 436SEM, DMS 441SEM, DMS 442SEM, EVS 317LEC, EVS 321LEC, EVS 327LEC, EVS 385LEC, EVS 418SEM, EVS 419SEM, EVS 442SEM, EVS 443SEM, EVS/SOC 341LEC
title: DMS 444SEM - Environmental Media Production

CSE 471LEC - Advanced Computational Linguistics

This course covers key areas in the field Computational Linguistics and considers current challenges for research in this domain, major application areas for automated language processing techniques, the skills needed to make use of language processing algorithms. The course is intended to expand on the content covered in LIN 467 /CSE 467 , and the precise topic coverage may be adapted to respond to student interest and emerging trends. This course is cross-listed with LIN 468 . 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

EVS 230LEC - Yellowstone Landscapes and Megafauna: Past and Present

Yellowstone Landscapes and Megafauna: Past and Present introduces students to the drama of life in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the only place in the lower 48 states where the full set of native big animals still roam. From the return of wolves in the 1990s to the ongoing battles between predators and prey, this course explores how animals shape the land and how the land, in turn, shapes them. Students will learn about Yellowstone’s natural history, food webs, succession, and ecosystem management while discovering why the park is often called the “Serengeti of North America.”

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: EVS 230LEC - Yellowstone Landscapes and Megafauna: Past and Present

MGM 120LEC - Foundations of Marketing

This course introduces students to the exciting world of marketing and helps them build a strong foundation for future study in the field. Designed especially for first-year marketing majors, it aims to spark curiosity about how marketing shapes the way we think, choose, and connect as consumers. Students will learn key marketing principles-such as understanding customer needs, creating value, and building lasting relationships-while exploring real-world examples that make marketing come alive. By the end of the course, students will not only understand what marketing is but also begin to see the world through a marketer’s eyes: curious, creative, and customer-centered.
 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: ECO 182 , PSY 101 , completion of or concurrent enrollment in MGG 102  or MGG 150 , marketing major only.
title: MGM 120LEC - Foundations of Marketing

CE 370LEC - Foundations of Nuclear Engineering

Fundamental nuclear science and engineering concepts forming the basis of contemporary nuclear technologies, including basic atomic and nuclear physics, special relativity, nuclear models and stability, nuclear reactions, radioactive decay processes, and neutron moderation and diffusion. Characteristics of nuclear radiation, and its detection, measurement, and interactions with matter. Nuclear safety, risk, regulation, and policy. Overview of reactor systems and materials, fuel production, biological effects of radiation, radioactive waste management, and fusion science and technology. A variety of practical and emerging applications are examined.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: CHE 107  and PHY 107 , Co-requisite: MTH 142 . School of Engineering and Applied Sciences Major or Nuclear Engineering Minor only.
title: CE 370LEC - Foundations of Nuclear Engineering

This course covers both qualitative and quantitative aspects of nuclear reactors for power production, preparing students to do basic design calculations and to make engineering decisions related to nuclear reactors.

Credits: 3

Graded (GRD)

Fall

Requisites:
Prerequisites: CE 370 , School of Engineering and Applied Sciences Major or Nuclear Engineering Minor only.
title: CE 470LEC - Introduction to Nuclear Reactor Engineering

MGM 416LEC - Principles of Category Management

This course introduces the principles and process of Category Management, a collaborative approach in which retailers and manufacturers work together to grow overall business performance. Students will learn how manufacturers can align with retailers’ objectives to build sales and profitability, with a focus on the Category Captain’s role in translating data into actionable insights. Through collaboration with a major retailer and leading manufacturers, students will apply the Nielsen Category Management suite and JDA space management software to develop and present a comprehensive Category Management Review.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Prerequisites: MGM 120  or MGM 301  , Business Administration students, Marketing major, and Marketing minor only.
title: MGM 416LEC - Principles of Category Management

MGM 412LEC - Marketing Analytics

This course offers an applied introduction to marketing analytics, focusing on how data and quantitative reasoning enhance decision-making in areas such as customer acquisition, retention, pricing, and promotion. Students will learn to use R to manage, visualize, and analyze marketing data, linking analytical techniques to strategic insights through a hands-on, “learning-by-doing” approach. Key topics include data visualization, exploratory analysis, A/B testing, segmentation, and regression modeling. By the end of the course, students will be able to structure analytical problems, apply appropriate methods, and communicate data-driven insights effectively.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: MGM 120   or MGM 301 , MGM 403 , Business Administration students, Marketing major, and Marketing minor only.
title: MGM 412LEC - Marketing Analytics

MGM 414LEC - Sales Leadership Analytics

This course focuses on developing analytical and decision-making skills for data-driven sales management. Students will learn to apply sales analytics methods, use data to drive decision-making and make sales teams more efficient and effective through the application of data. Real-world case work and a capstone project will allow the students to apply these new analytics skills.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: MGM 120  or MGM 301 , Business Administration students, Marketing major, and Marketing minor only.
title: MGM 414LEC - Sales Leadership Analytics

MGS 430LEC - AI Management Consulting

This course trains students to become future AI consultants and trusted advisors to organizations, big and small, seeking to harness and effectively integrate artificial‑intelligence technologies (generative AI and beyond) with business development techniques such as content creation, proposal generation, and value-based pricing to empower students to engage as a value added consulting partner. Students learn to bridge the gap between advanced technology and real-world business value. Students will learn to conduct comprehensive client needs assessments, design and propose tailored AI solutions, and guide businesses through responsible AI adoption. Students will learn how to partner with organizations to help identify business use cases, pain points, areas of growth and avenues for transformative technology innovation. Using current market research and industry frameworks to separate hype from reality, the course teaches participants to assess AI opportunities, design human‑AI symbioses, and craft workforce plans that account for reskilling needs and talent shortages. Students will learn to balance media and investor hype, using tools including the Gartner Hype Cycle framework to guide organizations through responsible technology investments, governed by enterprise risk appetite and management for new technology adoptions.  
 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Pre-Requisite: MGS 101  AND MGS 102 , OR MGS 351 , OR CSE 115  AND CSE 116
title: MGS 430LEC - AI Management Consulting

STA 125LEC - Data Clustering and Exploratory Data Analysis

This course introduces data clustering and exploratory data analysis (EDA). The course covers essential methods for visualizing and understanding data, including unsupervised learning techniques like k-means clustering, hierarchical clustering, and DBSCAN. Students will also learn how to explore datasets, detect patterns, identify outliers, and perform dimensionality reduction. Emphasis will be placed on using real-world datasets in the health sciences. Methods will be implemented in the R programming language. By the end of the course, students will be able to use EDA and clustering techniques to draw insights and inform data-driven decision-making.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Every other Fall

Requisites:
Prerequisites: STA 119  STA 119
title: STA 125LEC - Data Clustering and Exploratory Data Analysis

STA 245LEC - Statistical Learning with Applications in the R Programming Language

This course introduces supervised learning through hands-on examples in the R programming language. Topics include linear and logistic regression, subset selection, shrinkage methods, principal components, classification and regression trees, ensemble methods, and neural networks. Statistical aspects of model selection, validation, and reproducibility will be emphasized. High-dimensional applications will be highlighted.  This course includes “computational labs,” demonstrating methods and concepts in the R programming language using real data. Cutting-edge databases and packages such as Bioconductor, tidyverse, ggplot2, and plotly will be introduced in connection to workflow design.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Every other Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: STA 119  STA 119
title: STA 245LEC - Statistical Learning with Applications in the R Programming Language

html:
BE 421LEC - Biomaterials and Immune Response

This course explores the interactions between natural and synthetic materials and the human immune system. Students will examine the structure, properties, and functions of materials used in medical implants, as well as the biological tissues they interact with. The course covers the fundamentals of immune responses to foreign materials, mechanisms of biocompatibility, and the design principles for developing safe and effective biomedical devices. Additional topics include wound healing, inflammation, tissue engineering, and regulatory considerations for clinical translation. Through lectures, discussions, and critical analysis of current research, students will gain the knowledge and skills necessary to evaluate and design materials for medical applications with a focus on host response.

Credits: 3

Grading
GRD

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
BE 202 or (BIO 201 and BIO 211) and BE 305, School of Engineering and Applied Sciences Majors only
title: BE 421LEC - Biomaterials and Immune Response

html:
BMS 404LEC - AI & Neurodegenerative Disease, Medical Diagnosis and Treatment

Artificial intelligence (AI) models are capable of mapping physiological patterns to clinical impacts. In this course students will explore how multidimensional data can be leveraged in the diagnosis and treatment of neurodegenerative disease. It is becoming increasingly convenient to collect physiological signals from the human body using devices such as wearable sensors that can reflect physiological states and function of the body.  The goal of this course is to teach students about the principles of physiological structure-function relationships and how to apply machine learning and AI in the diagnosis and treatment of cognitive disorders, with a focus on neurodegeneration.  

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Prerequisites: BMS 301 , BMS 302
title: BMS 404LEC - AI & Neurodegenerative Disease, Medical Diagnosis and Treatment

html:
CE 150LEC - Science and Technology of Food: Chocolate, Spices, Beer, and More

An introduction to the chemistry, biology, physics, and technologies associated with food and cooking. Students investigate how atomic and molecular structure, intermolecular forces, and macromolecular behavior determine the texture, flavor, and transformations of foods during cooking. Science and technology topics addressed include water activity, protein denaturation, browning reactions, emulsions, pathogens, fermentation, distillation, sensory perception, and food preservation. Foods explored include milk, cheese, fruits, meat, custards, breads, seasonings, beer, coffee, and sweets. Emphasis is placed on data analysis, scientific reasoning, and evaluating food-related claims. Ethical issues in food science, sustainability, and misinformation are also discussed. Designed for non-science majors.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: CE 150LEC - Science and Technology of Food: Chocolate, Spices, Beer, and More

html:
EAS 394LLB - Problem Elaboration & Framing and Project Planning

This course is designed to develop skills and strategies related to problem framing and project planning. It adopts the notion that “design is widely considered to be the central or distinguishing activity of engineering ” and “that the purpose of engineering education is to graduate engineers who can design.” In this vein, the course is motivated by evidence from the engineering education literature that suggests: 1) novice designers often struggle to frame problems, instead moving ahead with solving the problem before it is fully understood; and 2) that an ability to “devise process” - planning and management of project work and coordination of a range of professional competencies - is important to the professional preparation of engineers but is not well integrated in undergraduate curricula.
  
This course will support student recognition and development of these components of professional practice through a problem- to project-based learning experience.
 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: EAS 394LLB - Problem Elaboration & Framing and Project Planning

html:
LAW 323LEC - Understanding Cyberlaw

Understanding Cyberlaw provides an in-depth examination of cybersecurity law as a rapidly evolving legal field governing digital risk, data protection, and cyber incidents across the public and private sectors privacy in the United States and internationally. The course explores the legal duties of organizations, professionals, and regulators in preventing, managing, and responding to cybersecurity threats. Designed for students without prior legal or technical background, the course offers lectures combined with active learning through class discussions (not cold call), simulations, and group presentations.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Every other Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: LAW 101
title: LAW 323LEC - Understanding Cyberlaw
