PAS 301LLB - Human Anatomy for Nursing Students

PAS 301 is designed for the first-year nursing student.  It provides a detailed overview of human anatomy from the cellular to the systemic level with an emphasis on the relationship between structure and function.  Course content is contextualized to common clinical practices with an eye towards preparing students for graduate studies and the clinic.

Credits: 4

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Nursing majors only.
title: PAS 301LLB - Human Anatomy for Nursing Students

html:
DEE 412SEM - Equity and Inclusion from Engineering Education to Practice

Equity and inclusion within engineering education bears implications for the diversity of the field, and likewise for engineering practice and beyond. In this course designed for non-majors, we will explore the interconnected consequences of culture, policies, practices, and more on equity and inclusion. We will examine the historical and systemic barriers that underrepresented groups face in entering and succeeding within the engineering field, and the broader impact these challenges have on workforce diversity. We will investigate the long-term, systemic effects of inequitable access to engineering education on innovation, societal progress, and the global workforce. The course will also address the consequences of these disparities for community well-being and access to engineering-driven solutions. By the end of the course, participants will have gained a deeper understanding of how fostering equity and inclusion within engineering education can lead to more inclusive, innovative, and socially responsible engineering practices that benefit diverse communities.
 

This course is dual-listed with DEE 512.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
School of Engineering and Applied Sciences Major only.
title: DEE 412SEM - Equity and Inclusion from Engineering Education to Practice

MAE 430LEC - Bioinspired and Biomimetic Engineering

The unique topics and expert guest line-up for this course promise to provide a great insight into the latest trends in this fast evolving and exciting field. There will also be exceptional opportunities to hear from NASA’s Nature Inspired Program, Grand Challenges, or many other cutting edge on-Earth or Space developmental activities in the field, such as bioinspired robotics and planetary, surface or ocean explorations, human missions and settlement plans, and DNA research and anti-aging in conjunction with future astronaut programs, etc.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Spring

School of Engineering and Applied Sciences majors only.
title: MAE 430LEC - Bioinspired and Biomimetic Engineering

MAE 463LEC - Additive Manufacturing

This course introduces the fundamentals of the additive manufacturing (AM) processes applied to various materials. The course also covers the design, analysis, and applications of AM technology and the factors affecting structure quality and functionality.

 

This course is dual-listed with MAE 563.

title: MAE 463LEC - Additive Manufacturing

BMS 403LEC - AI in Health Research and Clinical Care

This course introduces the concepts, technologies, and methods that underpin health informatics, with a special emphasis on wearable data.  Students will learn how devices collect health data, how this data is processed and integrated into healthcare systems, and the ethical considerations surrounding its use. Practical application and a final project will provide hands-on experience in analyzing wearable data and designing integration workflows.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring

Requisites:
Pre-requisites: BMS 301 , BMS 302
title: BMS 403LEC - AI in Health Research and Clinical Care

html:
MIC 416LEC - Immunotherapy and Microbial Therapeutics

Immunotherapy and Microbial Therapeutics examines how microbial and immune systems can be leveraged to prevent and treat disease through modern therapeutic and bioengineering strategies. Students will explore antibody and cellular immunotherapies, vaccine and vector platforms, and the design of live microbial therapeutics. The course emphasizes molecular and physiological mechanisms-how microbes survive and interact with hosts, how immune pathways can be modulated, and how biomanufacturing and synthetic biology enable scalable therapeutic development. Through analysis of primary literature and clinical case studies, students will evaluate current technologies, address biosafety and ethical considerations, and propose innovative therapeutic solutions grounded in microbial and immune system biology. The course emphasizes the translational pathway from biological discovery to therapeutic development and clinical implementation.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Pre-requisites: BIO 201  and CHE 201  or BIO 201  with BIO 211  and CHE 201  or permission of instructor.
title: MIC 416LEC - Immunotherapy and Microbial Therapeutics

html:
APY 107LAB - Introduction to Human Evolution Lab

This laboratory course provides a hands-on introduction to the scientific study of human evolution through the methods and practices of biological anthropology. Students will actively explore how evolutionary theory explains the emergence and diversification of our species by working directly with data, materials, and comparative specimens. Laboratory activities emphasize the formulation and testing of hypotheses, data collection and analysis, and interpretation of genetic, morphological, behavioral, and fossil evidence. Topics include the mechanisms of evolution, human genetic and phenotypic variation, primate anatomy and behavior, fossil reconstruction, and the material culture record from early primates to Homo sapiens. By engaging in laboratory investigations, students will gain practical experience in observing, measuring, and interpreting evidence that informs our understanding of human origins and evolutionary processes.

Credits: 1

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring

Requisites:
Corequisite: APY 107
title: APY 107LAB - Introduction to Human Evolution Lab

html:
APY 351SEM - Global Migrations: Mapping Human Mobilities

The course will provide an interdisciplinary overview of the geographies, economies and politics of human migration and transnational lives, even as we scrutinize the lenses through which immigration and migrant populations have been studied. A key intent is to understand the reasons behind the displacement and dislocation of individuals and populations as well as the processes involved in recent human mobilities. Our analysis of the present will be anchored in interdisciplinary historical perspectives. The course will also touch upon the reciprocal impact migration has on “host” spaces and on the places from which migrants originate. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Every other Spring
title: APY 351SEM - Global Migrations: Mapping Human Mobilities

html:
BIO 326LLB - Biodiversity & Speciation

What is the evolutionary and ecological origin of species? This course will explore the organismal biology behind the fundamental process of speciation, where new species are formed. We will discuss topics like geographic mode of speciation, ecological innovation in adaptive radiations, social behavioral effects on species boundaries, and the genomic barriers counteracting hybridization at species boundaries. The lab component (field trips, lab behavioral studies, and statistical modeling) will substantiate these profound processes with the forest creatures in Buffalo, NY, to gain a substantial understanding of the precious living organisms around us and how they came to be over millions of years of evolution. Join us on this dazzling and biodiverse journey!
Expected learning outcome: Establish an advanced understanding of the evolutionary and ecological principles behind biodiversity. Develop quantitative, analytical, and critical thinking to effectively understand speciation and biodiversity, starting from the organisms living around us.

Credits: 4

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall

Requisites:
Prequisites: BIO 200
title: BIO 326LLB - Biodiversity & Speciation

CHE 305LEC - Green Chemistry

This is a semester-long course designed to introduce the principles of green chemistry to reduce or eliminate the production of hazardous substances. Students will also be introduced to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The curriculum will cover how the principles of green chemistry can be developed to address global environmental and human health issues. Case Studies are used to provide relevant examples of green manufacturing processes and applications and to further reinforce chemical principles introduced in previous courses.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Every other Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisites: CHE 203  or CHE 251
title: CHE 305LEC - Green Chemistry

This course will provide a molecular and atomistic understanding of soft and solid-state materials, including inorganic solids, polymers, organic-inorganic hybrids, and low dimensional materials.

Graded (GRD)

Every other Spring

title: CHE 325LEC - Chemistry in the Solid State

html:
COM 459SEM - The triad of wellbeing: Connecting human, nature, and AI

As we merge more deeply with algorithmic systems, our relationship with biological reality is being radically rewritten. This interdisciplinary seminar triangulates three critical and evolving domains-Homo sapiens, the living Earth, and artificial intelligence-through the overarching theme of wellbeing. Interrogating the dichotomy between our immersion in digital spaces and our estrangement from the natural world, we examine how emerging technologies such as AI affect planetary and human health, exploring strategies for individual and collective action. From the materiality of the cloud to technobiophilia and interspecies communication, students will identify pathways where technology serves, rather than severs, our connection to the more-than-human world.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: COM 459SEM - The triad of wellbeing: Connecting human, nature, and AI

html:
PHI 351LEC - Philosophy and Political Economy of Free Expression

This course focuses on the nature of ethical and political aspects of free expression. The first part of the course covers foundational texts on the value and justification of free expression. The second part examines the legal and ethical limits of free speech. Part three of the course explores how free expressions drives the growth of knowledge in society. And part four studies current challenges to free expression in the form of polarization, misinformation, and social media.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: PHI 351LEC - Philosophy and Political Economy of Free Expression

html:
PHI 352LEC - American Dynamism

This course explores the institutional, cultural, and constitutional sources of flourishing. Part I introduces the idea of social dynamism and the growth of knowledge. Part II examines the connection between economic prosperity and dynamic evolution of the economy. Part III attempts to locate the explanation of economic dynamism in the legal or institutional structure of a nation, an idea expanded on in part IV, which surveys ideas of openness and relates them to social change. Finally, part V considers risks that dynamic societies face along with solutions that might address these risks.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: PHI 352LEC - American Dynamism

html:
PSY 454LEC - Child and Adolescent Development in the Digital Age

This course focuses on child and adolescent development in the digital age, with a particular emphasis on how rapidly advancing technologies, including Artificial Intelligence, video games, and social media, reflect, shape, and interact with contemporary child and adolescent socio-emotional development and well-being. We will examine core theories in social and emotional development and consider measures and methods in digital research. Current empirical findings pertaining to technologies and socio-emotional development during different developmental periods (infancy and toddlerhood, childhood, adolescence) and parenting will also be presented, along with careful consideration of the ways in which diverse technologies impact diverse groups of youth and how they develop today.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Every Other Fall

Requisites:
Psychology majors only. At least 45 credits completed.
title: PSY 454LEC - Child and Adolescent Development in the Digital Age

SSC 409SEM - Childhood Trauma and Adversity

This course provides an interdisciplinary exploration of trauma-informed care practices and the impact of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) on individual and community health outcomes. Students will examine the neurological, physiological, psychological, and social effects of childhood trauma. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring

Requisites:
Prerequisite: SSC 103
title: SSC 409SEM - Childhood Trauma and Adversity

html:
SSC 453SEM - Humane Technology and AI

Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming the way professionals in the social sciences and health and human services understand and respond to complex human needs. Students will trace the historical arc of AI to understand how past innovations inform today’s tools, while critically examining how practitioners are leveraging AI to improve client outcomes, inform policy, and address systemic challenges. A central focus of the course is developing a practical framework for assessing generative and non-generative AI systems, weighing their accuracy, potential for bias, and real-world utility in these high-stakes professional contexts. Whether pursuing careers in education, clinical environments, or in the nonprofit sector, students will leave with transferable skills and conceptual tools applicable across the full spectrum of human services settings. The course culminates in a group project in which student teams collaborate with a local organization to design and justify an AI-enhanced solution to a genuine community challenge.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: SSC 453SEM - Humane Technology and AI

html:
AHI 220LEC - Art Party: Renaissance Art, Costume, and Celebration

Celebrations such as festivals, ceremonies, and masquerades played an important role in the crafting of cultural identity in the early modern period (1400-1800). Parties promoted the creation of new and exciting artworks and gave artists license to experiment. In this course, students explore the artistic, architectural, and sartorial aspects of celebration. Situated in both courtly and community contexts - including royal weddings with elaborate fireworks displays and folk carnivals filled with costume, song, and dance - we uncover the ideologies embedded in large-scale celebrations that often occurred in urban spaces. We interrogate the term ‘Renaissance’ and expand beyond the European contexts often associated with it, noting how celebrations connected global cultures in the interwoven world of the 15th-18th centuries. Through paintings, popular prints, masks and costume, ephemeral architecture, fireworks displays, cultures of feasting and drinking, and more, we explore how celebrations defined/defied social norms and upheld/subverted political narratives.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: AHI 220LEC - Art Party: Renaissance Art, Costume, and Celebration

DAC 336SEM - Dance Studio MFA Thesis

This course will prepare students for performance in the MFA Thesis concert as a part of their career professionalization. Dancers will work closely with their choreographer to understand the unique physical and artistic challenges and expectations of the choreographic work. The culmination of the course will be the MFA Thesis production. 

Credits: 1-3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: DAC 336SEM - Dance Studio MFA Thesis

html:
LAW 321LEC - The Environmental Impact of War

This course focuses on the physical, chemical and biological effects that war and political conflict have on the environment. Topics will include ancient, historical and contemporary case studies and will span the globe. Examples include: the American conflict in Vietnam, deforestation, munitions pollution, Iraqi oilfields, and Sherman’s March to the Sea. This course is the same as EVS 321  and course repeat rules will apply. Students should consult with their major department regarding any restrictions on their degree requirements.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: LAW 321LEC - The Environmental Impact of War

html:
PHI 354LEC - Civil Discourse: Theory and Practice

Civil Discourse: Theory and Practice is an experiential course that develops the skills and habits required for productive disagreement in civic, professional, and public life. Students study major theories of deliberation, dialogue, negotiation, and democratic reasoning, then apply them through structured dialogues, facilitated discussions, simulations, and case-based exercises. Emphasis is placed on listening across difference, framing arguments for shared understanding, moderating contentious conversations, and negotiating principled compromises without erasing disagreement. Through repeated practice, reflection, and feedback, students learn to translate abstract concepts-such as legitimacy, reciprocity, power, and pluralism-into concrete communicative competence. The course is designed for students who want not only to understand civil discourse, but to practice it under real-world conditions of conflict, diversity, and uncertainty.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Spring
title: PHI 354LEC - Civil Discourse: Theory and Practice

html:
PHI 448LEC - PPE Research Lab

Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE) is an increasingly popular area of study. It brings together the analytic and normative tools of philosophy with the methods of the social sciences to get traction on meaningful, messy, high-stakes social and political problems. This PPE Research Lab is meant to be hands-on. Students will learn how to move from an interesting idea to a real research project: formulating a novel research question, choosing an appropriate method, and designing and executing a study-computational, experimental, or empirical. Along the way we’ll cover core elements of research design and build practical skills in computational modeling (including NetLogo). The class is also a workshop: students will regularly share work-in-progress, give and receive feedback, and practice the craft of constructive critique. 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: PHI 448LEC - PPE Research Lab

html:
PHI 339SEM - Ethics Bowl

The goal of this course is to provide you with a new level of competence at reasoning your way through moral/ethical problems. In order to accomplish that goal, we are going to aim at being successful at an activity called the Intercollegiate Ethics Bowl. While UB does not yet have an Intercollegiate Ethics Bowl team, the expectation is that this course will create interest for and eventually serve as part of the training for students who will participate in UB’s Intercollegiate Ethics Bowl team. Ethics Bowl is like debate, but instead of winning an argument, the goal is to engage as well as possible in collaborative thinking about real world ethical issues.

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall, Spring
title: PHI 339SEM - Ethics Bowl

html:
PHI 450LEC - Local Democracy in Action

What is democracy? How do democratic institutions at the local level differ from those at the state or national level? Who has power in the city of Buffalo? What should individuals and groups of residents do together to improve local democracy and solve collective action problems?

In this course, we will bring together tools from philosophy, politics, and economics to answer these questions. This course examines how residents, organizers, politicians and community groups work collectively to shape their cities and create positive change.  Focusing on Buffalo as our living laboratory, students will explore how democratic participation unfolds on the ground through organizing, coalition building, storytelling, and strategic action.
 

Credits: 3

Grading
Graded (GRD)

Typically Offered:
Fall
title: PHI 450LEC - Local Democracy in Action
